candidates.label: Damascus (historic city center)
candidates.support: Damascus has been continuously inhabited and identified at this location since antiquity; the old city, including the street called Straight, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

summary.text: Damascus lies in the northwest corner of the Ghuta, a fertile plain about 2,300 feet above sea level watered by the river Barada, the Abana of the Old Testament, and surrounded on three sides by bare hills, with open desert along its eastern edge. Among the most ancient cities of the Middle East, it had been part of the Roman province of Syria since the Roman general Pompey's conquest in 64 BC. In 2 Corinthians, Paul writes that around the time of his escape from the city, "the governor under King Aretas guarded the Damascenes' city, desiring to arrest me." How far the Nabataean king Aretas IV controlled Damascus at that time is debated; one proposal is that the Roman emperor Caligula gave him the city about AD 37. Aretas IV's reign ended in AD 40, so this record places Damascus within the Roman province of Syria for about AD 50.

history.text: Acts describes a light from the sky blinding Saul of Tarsus as he approached Damascus, and a voice identifying itself as Jesus; led by companions into the city, he was blind for three days until a disciple named Ananias, obeying a vision, restored his sight at a house on "the street which is called Straight." Saul, who became known as Paul, then preached in the city's synagogues that Jesus was the Christ, and his growing boldness provoked a plot to kill him: the Jews of the city "watched the gates both day and night," and Paul escaped by night, let down over the city wall in a basket.

Centuries later, the Umayyad caliphate made Damascus the capital of its empire, and the eighth-century Great Mosque of the Umayyads was built within the old city on the site of a Roman temple, over an earlier Christian basilica.

Today Damascus is a living city whose old quarter still follows the Roman street grid. Part of the ancient colonnaded street is still known as Derb el-Mustakim, "Straight Street," though it is uncertain whether it has carried that name continuously since antiquity. Visitors can also see the remains of the Roman Temple of Jupiter, stretches of the Roman city wall, and the Great Mosque of the Umayyads.

otConnections.note: Abraham pursues the kings who captured Lot as far north as the area of Damascus.
David defeats the Arameans of Damascus and stations a garrison there.
Isaiah's oracle states directly that Damascus is 'the head of Syria,' i.e. the capital of the kingdom of Aram.
The prophet Amos pronounces judgment on Damascus for threshing Gilead 'with instruments of iron.'
